direct_answer:
BASF states it conducted a double materiality assessment for the first time in accordance with the ESRS in 2024, building on prior assessments but with increased granularity and documentation, and plans to update it annually [Source 1]. The assessment was performed in three steps: (1) compiling a list of potential sustainability matters relevant to BASF’s business, customer industries and stakeholder groups, with particular attention to risk-prone parts of the business/value chain; the assessment was carried out at Group level along the value chain [Source 1]. Stakeholder interests were considered via direct inputs (e.g., Advisory Councils, BASF Civil Society Forum, multistakeholder networks) and indirect inputs (e.g., big data analyses of customer and capital market interests) [Source 1]. (2) BASF worked with in-house experts and selected stakeholders in its Nature Advisory Council and Human Rights Advisory Council to identify and validate risks and opportunities linked to impacts and dependencies, focusing on activities/sites/value-creation steps with elevated potential for negative impacts and risks; it also drew on its Group-wide opportunity and risk management system, into which material sustainability matters have long been integrated [Source 1]. (3) Impacts, risks and opportunities were scored using predetermined criteria on a 5-point scale and classified as material when exceeding defined thresholds; impacts were assessed for severity/scale/scope, with negative impacts additionally assessed for irremediability and potential impacts for likelihood; opportunities and risks were assessed for financial magnitude and likelihood, aligned with existing risk management methods, and prioritised by severity and likelihood [Source 3]. The assessment was reviewed iteratively by interdisciplinary experts and risk-reporting experts, and the Board of Executive Directors, Supervisory Board and employee representative bodies were informed of the process and outcome [Source 3]. After identifying material IROs, BASF mapped them to ESRS topic/subtopic/sub-subtopic and assessed ‘materiality of information’ at disclosure requirement/data point level using EFRAG criteria (decision-usefulness and stakeholder relevance) [Source 4].

Material sustainability matters identified as material from both an impact and a financial perspective are not explicitly listed in the retrieved passages. BASF does confirm that (i) climate change (E1) has multiple material impacts and also material climate-related risks and opportunities (i.e., financial perspective) [Source 5], (ii) biodiversity and ecosystems (E4) was defined as material (impact materiality is implied, but financial materiality is not evidenced in the retrieved text) [Source 8], and (iii) topics in ‘Own Workforce’ were defined as material and include risks for BASF (financial perspective) alongside impacts on employees [Source 12]. BASF also states ESRS S4 Consumers and End Users was assessed as not material [Source 2]. BASF notes that identified opportunities and risks have financial effects affecting financial position/performance/cash flow, and that in 2024 financial effects arose in connection with a risk identified under S3 Affected Communities [Source 2].
compliance_rationale: The passages provide substantial evidence on BASF’s double materiality assessment process, including value-chain scope, stakeholder inputs (direct/indirect), use of expert validation, linkage to enterprise risk management, and the scoring/threshold approach for impact and financial dimensions [Sources 1, 3, 4]. However, the retrieved passages do not provide a clear, complete list of sustainability matters that are material from both impact and financial perspectives; only partial topic-level indications (e.g., E1 climate change; Own Workforce; S3 financial effects; E4 materiality) are evidenced, without an explicit ‘both perspectives’ mapping across all material matters [Sources 2, 5, 8, 12].
disclosure_gaps: Explicit list of sustainability matters that are material from both impact and financial perspectives (double-material) in one place (topic-level mapping not fully evidenced in retrieved passages).
Clear identification of which topics are impact-material only vs financial-material only vs both (the retrieved text does not provide this classification).
Quantitative/qualitative definition of the ‘defined thresholds’ used to determine materiality (threshold values/criteria not disclosed in retrieved passages) [Source 3].

Evidence of engagement with affected stakeholders specifically across the overall DMA (beyond advisory councils/big data); for biodiversity, BASF explicitly states affected communities were not involved in identifying material topics [Source 8].
Comprehensive results table for all topics/subtopics (referenced as being on page 169, but not included in retrieved passages) [Source 5].
key_findings: BASF performed an ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment for the first time in 2024, at Group level along the value chain, and intends annual updates [Source 1].

Stakeholder interests were incorporated through direct engagement formats (Advisory Councils, Civil Society Forum, multistakeholder networks) and indirect big-data analyses (customers/capital markets) [Source 1].

Impacts were scored using severity/scale/scope (and irremediability for negative impacts; likelihood for potential impacts) and classified as material when exceeding thresholds; risks/opportunities were assessed by financial magnitude and likelihood, aligned with BASF risk management [Source 3].
Governance oversight included iterative expert review and informing the Board of Executive Directors, Supervisory Board and employee representative bodies [Source 3].
BASF reports E1 Climate Change has material impacts and also material climate-related risks and opportunities (indicating materiality in both dimensions for E1) [Source 5].
BASF states ESRS S4 Consumers and End Users is not material [Source 2].

Biodiversity and ecosystems (E4) was defined as material; BASF used stakeholder/specialist literature, internal experts, and digital/big data/AI tools, but affected communities were not involved in identifying material topics for this cluster [Source 8].
BASF indicates financial effects in 2024 arose in connection with a risk under S3 Affected Communities [Source 2].
